title: Properties, init, required and the field keyword
body: A property looks like a field to callers but runs accessor code. `public string Name { get; set; }` is an auto-property: the compiler creates a hidden backing field. Expression-bodied properties such as `public bool IsEmpty => Count == 0;` compute a value on each read. Prefer properties over public fields so you can add validation later without changing callers.

Accessors can have different accessibility (`public int Count { get; private set; }`). An `init` accessor allows assignment only during object creation, including object initializers and `with` expressions, then makes the property read-only. A `required` property must be set by every object initializer; forgetting it is error CS9035.

C# 14 adds the `field` keyword for field-backed properties: inside an accessor, `field` refers to the compiler-generated backing field. `set => field = value ?? throw new ArgumentNullException(nameof(value));` validates without declaring a separate private field. You may give a body to one accessor and leave the other as `get;`.

Because `field` is now a keyword inside accessors, an existing member actually named `field` must be written `this.field` or `@field` there. That is the C# 14 source-breaking risk to check when upgrading older code.

Property getters should be cheap and side-effect free; callers assume reading twice gives the same answer. Check that setters keep the object valid, that `init`/`required` express the construction contract, and that expensive work lives in a method whose name says so.

challenge: Add a Percent property to a Progress class using the field keyword so values below 0 become 0 and values above 100 become 100. Print the stored value after setting -5, 42 and 250.
question: Inside a C# 14 property accessor, what does `field` refer to?
correct: The compiler-generated backing field of that property
wrong: Any field named field declared in the class
A new local variable created for each call
reasoning: field lets you add logic to an auto-property without declaring the backing field yourself.
